extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers of literary theory and philosophy (including creative writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize conceptual standards and evaluative principles about imitation/representation (mimesis) in art and literature — how works should represent reality, use imitation, and achieve effects like catharsis or estrangement. Useful for literary students, critics, and creative writers thinking about 'showing' vs 'telling', realism, and techniques of imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation/Representation of Nature (mimesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Art as imitation or representation of nature (including human nature); mimesis conceived as the perfection and imitation of nature (Aristotle) and as a correspondence to the physical world as a model for beauty, truth, and the good (classical definition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle views art as reflecting nature and using mathematical ideas and symmetry to search for the timeless; art can present what is everlasting in contrast to nature's change. This standard suggests evaluating/producing work by its capacity to represent aspects of nature or human action in a way that reveals causes, patterns, or a 'timeless' significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show vs Tell (mimesis vs diegesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mimesis shows (directly represents action enacted), while diegesis tells (narration by a narrator who reports events).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In drama and enacted forms favoring mimesis, the action is presented 'here and now' rather than reported. For writers: prefer dramatization (dialogue, scenes, gestures) to narratorial summary when the goal is direct representation; use diegesis where authorial commentary or summarised account is appropriate. The page contrasts wholly imitative types (tragedy, comedy) with wholly narrative ones (dithyramb) and hybrid forms (epic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Catharsis: recognisability plus distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Catharsis (emotional purgation) arises only when the audience sees something both recognisable and sufficiently distant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle: the dramatist must create enactment that allows identification/empathy but preserves distance so the events do not happen to the audience. Practical implication: craft scenes that resonate emotionally and ethically with readers yet maintain narrative framing or emotional distance to prompt reflection rather than mere immersion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic structure and character standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy as 'an imitation of an action' characterized by a fall from a higher to a lower estate; tragic characters are posited as better than average while comedic characters are worse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing tragedy, design plot arcs that enact peripeteia (reversal) and place characters of elevated quality into circumstances that produce downfall; evaluate whether the action imitates a coherent moral or causal sequence that yields tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection, framing, and stylization in imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mimesis involves selecting elements from the continuum of experience and framing them; imitation often stylizes or exaggerates aspects of reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Michael Davis: imitation stylizes reality by selecting and giving boundaries to what is boundless. The frame signals that contained material is not simply real. Be aware that the more 'real' an imitation appears, the more 'fraudulent' it can become; craft involves purposeful selection and emphasis, not slavish duplication of every detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation versus copying (Coleridge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation diverges from mere copying: imitation consists in 'the interfusion of the SAME throughout the radically DIFFERENT, or the different throughout a base radically the same.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge's rule: avoid mere duplication of surface details; instead transform sources or experience so the work reveals underlying sameness of processes across different materialities. For writers: aim for imaginative transformation rather than literal transcription of speech or scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dionysian imitatio: imitation of earlier authors
rubrics_metrics.description: A literary method that emphasizes emulating, adapting, reworking, and enriching a source text by an earlier author (Dionysius of Halicarnassus); distinct from Aristotelian imitation of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard legitimizes deliberate borrowing, adaptation, and stylistic reworking of predecessors as a compositional technique. It implies evaluating derivative works by how well they rework sources (enrich, adapt, transform) rather than by whether they strictly replicate original form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verisimilitude / Realism as a representational goal
rubrics_metrics.description: Mimesis often identifies with realism or verisimilitude—the attempt to picture reality in its everyday sense (Auerbach).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a work's success in presenting a believable, internally coherent reality. Note philosophical debates: Lukács argued mimesis reveals social truth, while Brecht argued realism can dull the audience and advocated estrangement. Writers should choose between aiming for verisimilitude or intentionally breaking it for critical distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estrangement / Alienation effect (Brecht) as anti-mimesis technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Bertolt Brecht recommended using shock art and the estrangement effect to promote critical thought rather than passive identification with realist imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a compositional alternative to verisimilitude, employ techniques that prevent easy emotional absorption (breaking the fourth wall, didactic interruption, visible artifice) to provoke audience reflection and critique. Use as a deliberate counter to 'showing' that encourages uncritical empathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-consistency and internal rationalization (ludology/worldbuilding)
rubrics_metrics.description: In ludology and worldbuilding, mimesis refers to the self-consistency of a represented world and the availability of in-world rationalizations for its elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For speculative fiction, games, or constructed worlds, evaluate/produce settings that provide plausible in-world explanations for mechanics, puzzles, or oddities; higher mimesis equals greater internal logical consistency and fewer unexplained contradictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plato's critique: imitation vs truth and the danger of rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato argued poets and imitators lack 'techne' (knowledge) and are twice removed from truth; poetry can seduce and persuade by rhetoric rather than convey truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat mimicry with skepticism when claiming philosophical or moral truth; be aware that persuasive rhetorical technique can substitute for grounded knowledge. As a cautionary evaluative standard: question claims about 'truth' in works that rely primarily on rhetorical appeal rather than demonstrable understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimetic desire and social dynamics (Girard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Human behaviour is driven by mimesis; imitation of desires can engender rivalry and conflict with social and narrative consequences (René Girard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mimetic desire as a narrative device to depict competition, scapegoating, and escalation. Evaluate character motivations and plot dynamics for evidence of imitation-driven conflict and for how the narrative treats the productivity or destructiveness of such rivalry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimicry as political/strategic practice (postcolonial perspective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Postcolonial thinkers (Taussig, Bhabha) describe mimesis as a tactic by colonized or subordinate groups to camouflage and adopt characteristics of rulers as survival or preparatory rebellion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When portraying cultural imitation, assess sensitivity to reductionism and power dynamics. Use mimicry in fiction to explore identity, resistance, and the ambivalence of adopting another culture's signs; avoid simplistic portrayals that reduce mimicry to mere copying or inferiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperfect imitation as subversive/feminist tactic (Irigaray)
rubrics_metrics.description: Luce Irigaray describes imperfect imitation of stereotypes by women to expose and undermine those stereotypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a stylistic or performative device, imperfect or exaggerated mimicry can make oppressive norms visible and critique them. Consider deliberate over- or under-emphasis of stereotyped behaviour as a technique for political or feminist critique.
